blocks.text: …always in a stable connection
Definition and purpose 🐕

Distance interruptions are purposeful, practical exercises that enable us to interrupt our dog promptly during unwanted behaviour and bring it into a safe position at practically any time – across the distance of the long line and later, in free running, i.e. off-leash work, across large distances.
When in doubt, and with appropriate training, distance interruptions are an excellent alternative in practice to calling the dog back to us.
Used correctly, distance interruptions have a harmonising and de-escalating effect in many situations and therefore also serve to avoid conflict and to socialise the dog.

lessons.title: Sit and down at a distance

blocks.text: Definition and advantage 🐕

Distance interruptions using “Sit” and “Down” are suitable for situations in which our dog is at a greater distance from us and it would be impractical, impossible or even dangerous to call it back to us.
Distance interruptions allow us to secure our dog quickly while clarifying the situation at the same time.
Prerequisites and training basics 📋
Prerequisite: Our dog should respond to its name and have a basic command of the commands “Sit” and “Down”.

Training environment: The first training sessions take place without distraction. As training progresses, we apply the exercise with increasing distraction – but always only in such a way that, given the situation, it is foreseeable that the exercise can be completed successfully.
Leash: In the beginning we train on the leash. A minimum leash length of 4 metres is recommended.
Step 1: Addressing the dog 🗣️
While walking, we address our dog by name in a calm and firm tone of voice and stop at the same time. It is important that we do not trigger any state of alarm!
Step 2: Giving the command and walking towards the dog 👣
At the moment our dog responds – recognisable by stopping and looking at us – we calmly but firmly give the command “Sit” or “Down” and immediately walk towards it without interruption.

We walk briskly, but without startling the dog. While doing so, we repeat our command several times in an unexcited but binding tone. The aim is that the span of concentration between us and our dog is not broken.

As we approach the dog, we gather in the leash as we go so that it stays as slack as possible. Under no circumstances do we pull the dog towards us. Everything should proceed very firmly, but also harmoniously.
Step 3: Positioning and securing 📍

On reaching the dog, we bring it briskly and calmly into the “Sit” or “Down” position. We should preferably orient our dog towards the reliable “Down”. As long as “Down” is not yet sufficiently established, we can also use “Sit” – in future, however, “Down” should be the one mainly used, for reasons of reliability.

Note that the dog is brought into “Sit” or “Down” at the desired position with active help and does not first come back towards us to any notable extent. It is not wrong, and therefore not worth correcting, if the dog comes towards us in the first phase of training. As the learning effect increases, this behaviour fades and the dog goes into “Sit” and “Down” closer and closer to the time and place of the command.

The help is provided by calm guidance with the leash and by walking briskly towards the dog. The dog should then stay calmly in position and, if necessary, be corrected back into it quickly and convincingly if it gets up incorrectly.
Step 4: Waiting and ending the exercise ⏱️
Once the dog is lying or sitting, we calmly move away a few steps, later to the length of the leash, and leave it in position in its place for a certain time.
We end the procedure by calmly stepping up to the dog, pausing for a few seconds, and ending the exercise with “Sit” and intensive praise – optionally supplemented with play and a treat.

A calm sit in front of us ends the exercise. We take our time over the whole procedure and thereby teach the dog that “Sit” and “Down” at a distance are not a problem, and that carrying out the exercise in a safe position is a good alternative for feeling comfortable during encounters with people, dogs and other strong distractions.
Step 5: Progress and variations 📈

Once the procedure is established through regular daily training and the dog stays reliably in its place even when people and dogs walk past, we can move on to calling the dog to us after the encounter instead of fetching it.

This universally applicable socialisation exercise should be trained and applied whenever possible. Training off the leash in free running is only advisable once our dog carries out the exercise reliably on the leash under distraction without help from the leash.
The affectionate, calm praise at the end, supplemented with play and a treat as needed, puts our dog in a positive state of expectation, which places the next exercise on a successful foundation.
Distance and increasing the difficulty 📏
In this training, note that learning success depends on exercises running with little stress. We make a skilful choice between “Sit” and “Down”, depending on the expected difficulty of the situation.

At the beginning we choose a generous distance from the distraction. A good guideline is a distance of at least 10 to 20 metres – more for dogs that are easily distracted. As training confidence grows, this distance is reduced further and further until an interruption by “Sit” or “Down” is possible in close proximity to the distraction.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid harsh or loud commands during training and in everyday use.
Avoid keeping the leash short.
Avoid carrying out exercises in the direction of the distraction.
Avoid praising too early while the situation is still ongoing.
Avoid stress throughout the entire procedure.
Avoid the dog leaving the exercise position on its own.
Avoid ending the exercise too early, which would result in the dog breaking out of the situation uncontrolled.
Practical impulse: Confident at a distance

Begin by practising in a completely low-stimulus environment, at least 10 to 20 metres from the nearest distraction. With every command, walk towards your dog immediately and briskly – your movement is the key to the connection. With every distance interruption handled calmly, the stable connection between you and your dog grows, and it holds in free running as well.
→ Does our dog have a firm command of “Sit” and “Down”?
→ Do I train in distraction-free terrain in the early stages?
→ Have I ensured an undisturbed sequence?
→ Do I consistently train on the long leash for the first period?
→ Do I increase the training demands step by step towards application in situations with distraction?
→ Do I only switch to off-leash training when the leash is no longer needed to carry out the exercise?
→ Do I communicate with the dog calmly and bindingly?
→ Is my body work correct, and do I walk towards the dog with confidence?
→ Do I bring the dog into “Down” confidently and promptly?
→ Do I regularly leave the dog in position for a while?
→ Do I end the exercise calmly and with appropriate pauses, as described in the guide?
→ Do I praise generously afterwards?
